body.text: Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are set to meet in Shenzhen next week, and experts speculate that their discussions may focus on tariff reductions, additional agricultural purchases, and critical minerals. Positive outcomes would boost the stock market, highlighting not only their success, but also the success of two major governments that are increasingly playing a role in determining who gets to trade.

Easing trade tensions belie who reaps the benefits of these developments. Chinese state-owned enterprises may be induced by new policies to purchase large orders, even as private buyers continue to purchase goods elsewhere. Export restrictions may be relaxed, but businesses may continue to struggle to obtain licenses or find willing suppliers. Companies that have the resources and regulatory expertise to navigate this complex regulatory landscape may retain access to markets that remain difficult for others to enter.

Here is an example. After the October 2025 trade truce, China continued to make large purchases of U.S. agricultural products, particularly soybeans. As of late January 2026, Chinese state owned firms Sinograin and COFCO had purchased 12 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans. While this was indeed beneficial for American farmers, private Chinese processors continued to purchase from Brazil since it offered lower margins due to large differences in tariff rates. This indicated that ordinary commercial demand had not fully recovered.

Critical minerals provide another example. Also after the October 2025 negotiations, China paused export restrictions on critical minerals, delaying the implementation of some measures until January 2027. However, exports of rare earth compounds to the United States and Japan still declined by 58 percent in the ten months following the agreement compared with the ten months before, while exports to the rest of the world increased by 146 percent. This may be because some Chinese rare earth suppliers were afraid of regulatory or political repercussions in exporting to the United States.

U.S. technology restrictions have also resulted in lengthy export-license delays, unclear procedures, and lost business opportunities for American tech firms, including for products already available in China from other suppliers. The Nvidia controversy has drawn a massive amount of attention to U.S. tech export policy. After allegations involving former CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, lawmakers have called for tighter export control through passage of the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act, and MATCH Act, which would increase congressional oversight of advanced chip exports, strengthen measures against chip diversion, and encourage additional restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Even if Trump agrees to loosen export restrictions on U.S. technology as part of a deal with Xi, those concessions could prove short-lived if Congress tightens the rules.

U.S. importers paid a price for changing suppliers under Trump’s first term. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found that finding replacement foreign suppliers cost the average importer an equivalent of 5 percent of annual sales and that establishing new supplier relationships took more than two-and-a-half years on average. This shows that the impact of trade restrictions is not only the direct tariff cost, but also the cost of qualifying new suppliers or potentially moving production for companies that can afford to do so. Companies that cannot afford the additional indirect costs may lose contracts or be forced to withdraw from the market. Even after trade restrictions are lifted, businesses may not return to their previous supplier relationships, having already invested considerable time and money in establishing new ones.

For several decades, companies chose how they wanted to carry out China-U.S. trade, incentivized by costs and benefits. They operated under government rules, but firms generally had the freedom to determine how to develop their commercial relationships. In the past eight years or so, however, export controls, investment restrictions, tariffs, and government purchasing commitments have increasingly influenced which transactions are possible.

This does not mean that negotiations between the United States and China cannot produce valuable results. Lower tariffs or clearer export procedures could have large benefits, but the point is that these agreements should not be judged only at face value. Deeper analysis should be carried out to understand whether private buyers are returning alongside state-owned purchasers, how many firms are participating in bilateral trade, and whether approved licenses result in actual deliveries.

If commercial opportunities are dependent on a changing regulatory landscape, an apparent recovery in China-U.S. trade numbers might conceal reduced economic participation. Therefore, the real test of a Trump-Xi agreement will be not only how much trade it restores, but whether businesses can compete for and participate in that trade on workable commercial terms.
